https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2025/05.title: I refuse to live in Ed Miliband’s grim future, without showers or kettles
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2025/05.subtitle: The answer to climate change has never lain in the Energy Secretary’s vision of the world. We need something better, and fast
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2025/05.text:
Ed Miliband is obsessed. The Energy Secretary is fired by the same manic hubris, that messianism that brings traffic to a halt, wastes police time and ruins people’s days, as the loony green groups Extinction Rebellion and Just Stop Oil. As with so many eco-zealots, people, indeed those Labour was elected to serve, are fodder, expendable, to be swept aside, as the dystopian vision for Britain – a decarbonised grid in five years from now – is forced on us.
On Labour’s election, Miliband promised to “move fast and build things” to the tune of £40 billion in investment per year. By “building things”, might Miliband actually mean destroying things? One thinks here of the planned halting of North Sea oil and gas drilling licences whose main effects will be that we are left with greater dependency on enemy states for gas and, it is estimated, over 100,000 British jobs are lost.
Unsurprisingly, Miliband has become an increasing liability for Labour. His plan to rewire the whole national grid and power the country, in short order, with wind and solar – a process that will be full of faults, eyesores, and grievous noise and other nuisances – are at “the limits of what is feasibly deliverable”, according to the Government’s own National Energy System Operator. It’s embarrassing.
It also won’t work, not just because it is not “feasibly deliverable” but because this is still Britain, and we can’t be entirely railroaded by the eco lobby. I am no fan of Reform, but I did find a degree of satisfaction in the deputy chairman and Lincolnshire MP Richard Tice’s warning to Labour about its renewables plans for his region. “We will attack, we will hinder, we will delay, we will obstruct, we will put every hurdle in your way. It’s going to cost you a fortune, and you’re not going to win. So give up and go away.”
Critics raged about how such a view translates to wishing for the loss of thousands of jobs created by the net-zero infrastructure industry. But this is a bit like pointing to the cost of fire extinguishers when trying to stop Rome burning.
Naturally, it would be wonderful if the whole world could immediately stop making global warming worse, and find a way to reverse the damage already done. And maybe, had we put real money and effort into creative, technology-forward solutions when Margaret Thatcher began warning about climate change back in the 1980s, we would have.
But the current proposals are as pointless as they are dangerous. Britain, even as we are now, with minimal industry and a fast-diminishing farming sector, is hardly going to be make-or-break on this problem. The Americas, India, parts of Africa, the Arab world … these are the guys who could make a difference, but aren’t particularly bothered about doing so. In some cases, it’s the reverse.
Meanwhile, going full-tilt for net zero as Miliband desires is widely understood to be incredibly dangerous and a huge national security risk. Shutting down our own pipeline of gas means dependency on, and vulnerability to the likes of Russia, from whom we still import some gas, and Qatar, not exactly a liberal democracy, and a major exporter of natural gas to us.
Meanwhile, China makes 80 per cent of the world’s solar panels, and you can’t remake an energy grid in the image of Miliband’s dreams without being up to your ears in its monopoly on green energy. While Labour is busy cosying up to China, perhaps it should be thinking more about the American discovery of “communication devices” in Chinese-made solar power batteries and converters, which connect the panels to the grid. This equipment is capable of bypassing firewalls, with catastrophic national security consequences. Mike Rogers, a former director of the US National Security Agency, said: “We know that China believes there is value in placing at least some elements of our core infrastructure at risk of destruction or disruption.” This is a terrifying threat.
Yet Miliband and his fellow net-zero evangelists are choosing this future for Britain over one in which we can both boil the kettle when we want without fear of overtaxing the grid, and retain a degree of sovereignty, which will be handy when the next world war really gets into gear.
And the cost to us, modern people accustomed to life in the First World, of Miliband’s vision is simply unthinkable. We are, it seems, to begin to adjust to mass outages like that which brought Spain and Portugal to a standstill recently, due to an unexpected surge. Foul play by a foreign power has not been ruled out in that case either.
Haven’t we lived long enough in darkness, cold and hunger? The ability to have a hot shower, a freshly boiled kettle, bright light at will; to eat meat if meat is desired; to travel domestically and further afield however we choose, by car or plane or train … these are all things that we take for granted, and that we ought to take for granted. They are the rudiments and the building blocks of daily life in a civilised country.
It is one thing for green lunacy to be active at the fringes. But it is not right that net-zero fanaticism has been embraced so roundly at the very top, among political leaders in more than one party: it is not right in a historical context, nor by basic standards nor even by science, which requires a search for better explanations for problems, not pretending to solve them by hurtling us all back to the stone age.
We all want to find a way to reverse the damage to Earth and its atmosphere that has been caused by carbon emissions; this is important for billions of people’s way of life too. But the answer has never lain in the Miliband vision of the world. We need something better, and fast.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/world-news/2.title: Five years of virtue signalling: the failure of Black Lives Matter
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/world-news/2.subtitle: Footage of George Floyd dying under a police officer’s knee sparked outrage, protests and ‘gesture politics’, but real change takes more
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/world-news/2.text:
The infamous 8 minutes, 46 seconds (later revised by prosecutors to 9 minutes, 29 seconds) in which George Floyd, a Black American, lay dying under a white police officer’s knee in the streets of Minneapolis on May 25, 2020, seared itself onto the American conscience in a matter of hours.
Within a fortnight, silences lasting exactly the same period of time had been observed in the New York Stock Exchange, the United States Congress (where some Democrats draped themselves in Ghanaian kente cloth while they kneeled), and public vigils held across Britain.
By the beginning of July 2020, up to 26 million Americans are thought to have protested at more than 4,700 demonstrations. In the UK, hundreds of thousands of people attended sympathetic rallies from Bristol to Birmingham to Belfast, surpassing the numbers mobilising for Rock Against Racism in the Seventies. Worldwide, protests are thought to have taken place in 93 countries.
But it wasn’t just the raw statistics of the Black Lives Matter (BLM) protests that were so remarkable. It was also the arresting imagery of toppled statues; the powerful sloganeering of Floyd’s final words, “I can’t breathe”; and, for many, a new – and often confusing – lexicon of terms from “anti-racist” to “diversity, equity and inclusion”.
Then, it all seemed to evaporate almost as quickly as it had arrived. “The era of Black Lives Matter, Latinx, critical race theory, pronouns and defunding the police is over,” declared one columnist in the London Evening Standard (now The London Standard), on the morning of Trump’s election victory last November.
Five years on from those extraordinary events of 2020, what is George Floyd’s legacy in the USA and the UK?
Were BLM’s protests simply a “moment”, as Sir Keir Starmer “regretted” calling them in July 2020 (during a summer in which he flip-flopped between ‘taking the knee’ and promising to sign up for unconscious-bias training)? Or were they the start of a genuine movement that precipitated meaningful change?
A blunt assessment of BLM activists in America is that they achieved the exact opposite of what they set out to do.
Mathis Ebbinghaus, a Junior Research Fellow in sociology at Oxford University, has studied BLM by compiling data on police budgets between 2018 and 2021 for 264 major cities in the USA. “We found no evidence that BLM protests led to police defunding,” he explains. “In cities with large Republican vote shares, protest is associated with significant increases in police budgets.”
There was also a political dimension to the backlash against BLM. By campaigning to “defund the police” – a reductive slogan, labelled “the three worst words in the English language” by one Democrat, which summarised a complex programme of redistributing police funds towards social problems – BLM activists and some of their Democrat supporters had gifted the Republicans a 22-point advantage on handling crime by 2022.
The George Floyd Justice in Policing Act, which was intended to ban chokeholds, crack down on “no-knock” warrants and make it easier to prosecute criminal police officers, had already stalled in a partisan Congress the previous year. Facing the loss of the House at the mid-terms, Joe Biden resorted to signing an executive order that would apply some of the Act’s terms to federal officers. It was duly rescinded by Donald Trump on his first day back in office in January 2025 – although 24 states have passed their own laws banning or restricting chokeholds and four states have banned no-knock warrants. Two months later, Elon Musk urged the President in a tweet to “think about” pardoning Derek Chauvin, the police officer serving 22.5 years in prison for Floyd’s death.
Meanwhile, according to a database compiled by the Washington Post, American police have, on average, killed more than 1,000 people every year since 2015, with Black Americans killed at more than twice the rate of white Americans. In 2024, the total number of fatal police shootings reached a record high of 1,173.
“The problem with Black Lives Matter is that, compared to the Civil Rights Movement in the Sixties, with its focus on legislation and desegregation, it doesn’t really have a realistic solution,” says Michael Biggs, an Associate Professor of Sociology at the University of Oxford, who has a particular interest in the volatility of collective protest. “‘Defunding the police’ just didn’t work out. It was a utopian project to think that, if you could reduce the police numbers, violence would magically fall.”
Attempts at police reform in the UK have been slightly more realistic – but only marginally more successful.
Influenced by George Floyd’s murder, as well as the long-running distrust between the police and Black communities, the National Police Chiefs’ Council and the College of Policing launched a Police Race Action Plan (PRAP) in May 2022. Three years later, PRAP has pleased almost no one, despite its latest report pointing to some progress: twice as many staff dismissed for discriminatory behaviour in 2022/2023 than in 2020/2021; a falling rate of stop and search and use of force on those from Black backgrounds; and a growing percentage of Black officers.
To critics on the Right, PRAP is an overreaction to what was, at heart, an American problem, the different cultures perhaps best illustrated by British protestors shouting the BLM slogan “Hands up, don’t shoot” at unarmed Metropolitan Police in June 2020.
“Police chiefs have got themselves into an awful muddle,” says David Spencer, Head of Crime and Justice at Policy Exchange and a former Detective Chief Inspector. “They have committed themselves to a specific, ideological form of anti-racism, but that is a political position, whereas the core of policing is keeping the public safe and catching criminals. We’re seeing good operational officers working in fear of being called racist – and that position does no one any good. The idea that communities are being ‘over-policed’ when Black children are murdered on the streets is utterly pernicious.”
Meanwhile, many on the Left are frustrated by what they see as a missed opportunity to reform policing.
“Since George Floyd’s murder, we’ve seen the introduction of increasingly punitive policing legislation giving police more powers to criminalise protest and marginalised communities,” says Dr Remi Joseph-Salisbury, an anti-racism activist and Reader in Sociology at the University of Manchester. “People were calling for serious investment in communities and for alternative visions of safety, but they were often dismissed out of hand.”
“There is a widespread view that we have not delivered tangible change,” admitted Chief Constable Gavin Stephens, the Senior Responsible Officer for PRAP, in a report published earlier this year. “This reflects the feelings from our partners at the National Black Police Association, who fear that the wider landscape for both their members and out in our communities is now worse than when this plan was launched.”
A similar Left-Right divide can be seen in the political response to Floyd’s death. In June 2020, Boris Johnson appointed Tony (now Lord) Sewell to look at “all aspects of inequality”, despite recommendations from the Lammy Review (2017) and the Windrush Review (2020) already sitting on the shelf. To general apoplexy on the Left – an academic compared him to Joseph Goebbels; a Labour MP tweeted a picture of a Ku Klu Klan member – Sewell reported the following year that, although racism still persisted, race relations had improved significantly, and that the main causes of race disparity were class and geography, not race.
“If you’re talking about race, you also have to talk about white people,” says Sewell, whose report found that the worst outcomes were among low-income white groups. “It’s not about identity politics or a league table of victimhood; it’s about people’s material conditions. If the Tories had really grasped that document and ran with it, they would have found a cause célèbre for their levelling-up project.”
The main way in which people in Britain engaged with George Floyd’s death was not, of course, through reports compiled long after the event but through the immediacy of social media.
“The Covid lockdown partly explains the magnitude of the response,” says Professor Biggs. “People were inside their homes looking at that shocking video. If you’re a young person living online, you’re living in an American world. On social media, we’re effectively a colony of the United States.”
Eager to do something to demonstrate their support for racial justice, millions of social media users posted black squares on their profiles in June 2020 in a global campaign known as Blackout Tuesday. Other forms of public solidarity included “taking the knee”, an anti-racist gesture popularised by an American football player in 2016 and widely adopted in the English Premier League between 2020 and 2022 (this season it has still taken place before specific matches, to demonstrate an “ongoing commitment to fight racism and all forms of discrimination”). This led to the strange spectacle of the England football team kneeling before their World Cup match in 2022, while their American opposition remained standing.
Sir Keir Starmer famously released a photo of himself and Angela Rayner “taking the knee” in his Commons office in June 2020, and Alan Pughsley, then Chief Constable of Kent Police, was among officers who knelt alongside activists. Priti Patel, then Home Secretary, dismissed the practice as “gesture politics”. Even sympathisers of BLM worry that performance often took the place of substance.
“Taking the knee, sharing a black square or issuing a corporate statement means very little without real change behind it,” says Dr Joseph-Salisbury. “In many cases, those gestures actually worked to contain and neutralise the political power of the moment. For example, Keir Starmer took the knee publicly, but at the same time dismissed defunding the police as ‘nonsense’ – showing a clear disconnect between symbolism and substance.”
This virtue signalling, much of it doubtless well-meaning, reached its apogee in the corporate world, where it has also seen the biggest backlash in recent months.
Within three years of Floyd’s murder, companies had pledged more than $340 billion to combat racial injustice by setting diversity targets, hiring dedicated staff and launching new training programmes.
“The impact of George Floyd’s death and the BLM movement on workplace DEI [diversity, equity and inclusion] was profound,” says Sandi Wassmer, CEO of the Employers Network for Equality & Inclusion. “Employers began to recognise the impact of structural and systemic racism across all areas of the employee life cycle, from recruitment and retention to development and progression.”
Not all employees were delighted, however, by the implications of this recognition.
“With DEI, you’re on the clock for your soul,” says Joanna Williams, a former academic and author of How Woke Won. “BLM ushered in a woke authoritarianism. It allowed DEI officers to assume a sense of moral superiority and, with it, the authority to monitor and regulate how people speak, think and feel.”
By 2024, there were signs of a significant slowdown in the DEI boom, with jobs in the sector experiencing an attrition rate that was double that of other positions. Chinny Okolidoh, the BBC’s first Director of Diversity & Inclusion lasted less than two years in the role – and wasn’t replaced when she left last year.
The USA took the lead in the backlash – culminating in the election of Trump, who issued a raft of executive orders in January that rolled back DEI in the public and private sectors. To date, the UK hasn’t followed suit, although a poll in March by the Institute of Directors revealed that 11 per cent of companies intend to scale back diversity activities in the near future.
“There has always been an anti-DEI, anti-woke brigade in the UK, but employers cannot abandon DEI work altogether,” says Wassmer. “We have far stronger employment and equality legislation so, at a minimum, employers will still need to comply.”
One of the stranger consequences of George Floyd’s death was the statue wars that affected countries from New Zealand to India. In the United States, more than 160 Confederate tributes were removed from public spaces. In the UK, before Historic England introduced its “retain and explain” policy in 2021, almost 70 memorials to colonialists were removed or altered. Famously, these included the statue of Edward Colston, the Bristol slave trader, which was thrown into the city’s harbour by BLM activists in June 2020.
Polling at the time showed a significant split in public opinion, with one YouGov survey finding that only 13 per cent of people approved both of Colston’s statue being removed and the way in which it was carried out. Meanwhile, 40 per cent of respondents approved of its removal, but not in the way in which it was done, while a third disapproved entirely.
Three years later, these wars were given another lease of life by the Public Order Act, a culmination of the Conservative government’s anger at similar attacks on monuments, alongside an increase in protests by groups such as Extinction Rebellion and Just Stop Oil. The legislation introduced a maximum prison sentence of 10 years for criminal damage to a statue.
In 2025, however, there has been a quieter return to the status quo ante bellum. Last month, a plaque was installed on Colston’s empty plinth. In March, another of Trump’s executive orders sought to reinstate almost 100 Confederate monuments. Meanwhile, only one block away from the White House, government workers began removing a giant “Black Lives Matter” slogan with jackhammers.
It’s difficult not to conclude, therefore, that BLM has suffered serious setbacks on almost every front, from politics to police reform, the boardroom to the classroom – where its embrace of “critical race theory”, a widely misunderstood explanation of systemic racism, triggered a fierce backlash in America from a combination of parents, podcasters, state legislatures and Fox News.
A disparate organisation, split into local chapters with a range of grievances and aspirations, BLM raised $90 million in 2020, only to see its funds slow to a trickle five years later. Meanwhile, its support among Americans fell from 67 per cent in 2020 to 51 per cent in 2023. The organisation did not respond to The Telegraph’s requests this week for comment.
“Ultimately, the achievements of BLM were rather miniscule,” says Professor Biggs. However, its critics continue to worry that the damage has already been done.
“What we’re seeing is a backlash against the excesses of BLM,” says Williams. “We look back now and it seems like a lot of people went crazy in 2020. It coincided with Stonewall reigning supreme, with Mermaids UK [a transgender charity] sending speakers into schools. So the backlash is not so much against the ideas underpinning all this, but against the extreme forms they took. You can row back on the excesses, you can take down your BLM sign, but the underlying identity politics is relinquished far less readily.”
And, of course, not everyone has taken down their BLM sign.
“Their legacy is complex,” says Dr Joseph-Salisbury, who is a steering group member of a “police abolitionist group” in Manchester. “On the one hand, the uprisings galvanised people, built momentum, and brought many into anti-racist movements for the first time. On the other hand, the backlash has been fierce. In the UK, we’ve seen the state doubling down: anti-protest laws, attacks on migration and attempts to erase institutional racism from the public conversation. This has not abated with the change of government.
“But there’s still hope in the grass roots – in local organising, in mutual aid, in youth activism. The legacy may not lie in what governments did, but in the communities and movements that continue to push for justice. The ideas at the heart of BLM – about justice, safety and dignity – remain urgent, and they’re still being fought for. Progress isn’t always linear or immediate, and its effects can take time to bear fruit.”
To put it another way: it takes longer to decide a man’s legacy than it does to kill him.

author: Iain Hollingshead

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2025/05.title: Good riddance to Carla Denyer: wrong about everything, all the time
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2025/05.subtitle: If the Greens have any sense, they’ll appoint as next co-leader someone who knows what a woman is
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2025/05.text:
It was during an interview with LBC’s Tom Swarbrick when Carla Denyer – who has just announced she is stepping down as co-leader of the Greens – came unstuck.
Imagine an Extinction Rebellion protester glued to the M1 being ripped out of their own trousers by an irate commuter and then forced to stand in the honking traffic in their underwear.
When asked “does living like a woman make you a woman?”, the MP for Bristol Central, 39, (pronouns she/her), appeared completely baffled.
“I trust people to be an expert in their gender,” she insisted. “If someone has been living as a woman for 15 years…”
“What does that mean, living as a woman?” interrupted Swarbrick, not unreasonably.
“Well it means what I said,” replied Denyer, despite everything she’d said making no sense at all.
Granted, the Greens have been electorally successful under Denyer and her co-leader Adrian Ramsay, who was elected as the MP for Waveney Valley last July.
As she crowed in her departure statement, released to the Guardian (obvs): “We’ve achieved so much, taking the party from one MP to four, from 450 councillors to over 850, and winning nearly 2m votes at the last general election.”
But at what cost to good, old fashioned, common sense? An ecostremist who refused to put her student politics behind her, Denyer was one of the chief architects of green hysteria, bringing about a European first in 2018 when she managed to persuade Bristol City Council to declare a “climate emergency”. Had she persuaded Beijing, rather than Bristol, it might have had more impact on the world’s CO2 emissions, but on she Thunberg’d.
Desperate to score a full house on the Just Stop Oil bingo card, she railed against the use of fossil fuels (despite having a gas boiler rather than a heat pump in her own home), campaigned against the expansion of Bristol Airport (despite the jobs and economic benefits it would bring to the local area) and lobbied to introduce congestion charging in Bristol (despite the Green council later abandoning the idea in favour of a “workplace levy”).
Not content with voters facing the biggest tax burden in peacetime, on top of a cost of living crisis, she also called for the city to raise the top band of council tax – and has regularly advocated for the introduction of a wealth tax.
In a typically prescient statement in 2024, Denyer insisted: “The claim that wealth taxes would lead to large numbers of people leaving the UK isn’t credible.”
Figures now show that one millionaire left Britain every 45 minutes in the year Labour came to power, with the UK losing 10,800 millionaires to overseas countries in 2024, more than double the number in 2023.
Denyer says she is standing down as co-leader to “pour all of my skills, passion and energy into being the best MP I can be, in parliament and in Bristol Central.” Presumably this will also allow her to keep campaigning on such local issues as “ending the illegal occupation of Gaza” and “stopping arms sales to Israel”.
She will certainly be in good company, since on Denyer’s watch, the Greens have allowed committed environmentalists like Mothin Ali to be elected as local councillor to shouts of “Allahu Akbar”. Ali, a keen gardener, described a local Rabbi as a “kind of animal”. The Jewish university chaplain, his wife and children were forced into hiding. Ali also labelled Israel “white supremacists” following the October 7 attacks and claimed Gaza was “the biggest concentration camp the world has ever seen”. Eco-friendly stuff.
With a track record of being wrong about everything, all the time, it will come as no surprise that Denyer reacted to the Supreme Court ruling that trans women are not, in fact women, with a piece in the Pink News declaring interim guidance published by the Equality and Human Rights Commission to be a “bigot’s charter”.
You read that right folks – the EHRC, that’s the body responsible for promoting and enforcing equality in the UK – is, according to Denyer, now a vehicle for bigotry. (One assumes she means an electric vehicle. Incidentally, the virtue signalling Greens appear to have said precious little on the use of Uyghur slave labour to make EVs, solar panels and components for wind farms in Britain).
A bisexual, vegan “nonthesist Quaker”, Denyer opened her maiden speech by stating her preferred pronouns, in what she believed to be a parliamentary first. If the Greens have any sense, which seems unlikely, they’ll perhaps consider appointing someone who knows what a woman is to replace her.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/business/202.title: Now even Greenpeace is worried about North Sea oil jobs
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/business/202.subtitle: We are told net zero will create employment, but there’s no sign of it happening
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/business/202.text:
Even by the standards of Greenpeace and Unite it was a very odd protest. A coalition of 60-plus environmental and union groups staged a demonstration outside Parliament this week demanding a huge programme of government spending to help North Sea oil workers laid off by the closure of the fields.
But hold on. Weren’t we told there were going to be lots of well-paid green jobs? Surely the workers made redundant on the rigs can just get one of those?
There is just one problem. It is becoming painfully clear that the green jobs revolution promised by Ed Miliband, the Energy Secretary, is a self-serving fantasy – and tens of thousands of genuinely well-paid jobs are being pointlessly sacrificed.
In a week when the legislation to create Great British Energy, the Labour Government’s state-owned renewables champion, was finally passed through Parliament, we should all be welcoming the wave of green jobs that are about to be created, along with the lower energy bills that should be coming our way very soon.
“As part of our Plan for Change, this will make us a clean energy superpower and help bring down energy bills for good,” argued Miliband as the legislation was passed. Well, perhaps. It seems, however, that no one got around to telling all the workers in the North Sea who will soon be losing their careers.
As the bill was passing through Parliament, a group of protesters gathered outside to demand that as well as the £8bn being spent on GB Energy, another £1.9bn of taxpayers’ money should be used to create new jobs for all the people about to be laid off from the oil and gas rigs in the North Sea.
“Offshore workers have risked life and limb and suffered long stints away from their families to keep this country moving and it’s time the Government repaid their sacrifices with an industrial strategy that puts worker justice at its heart,” according to Greenpeace.
Seriously? Green campaigners are worried about workers on oil rigs?
For years now we have been lectured on how the transition to greener energy would create lots of jobs. Now we are being told that everyone laid off in the traditional energy industry will be unemployed if the Government doesn’t step in to help them.
In reality, the contradiction only makes sense when you realise one very simple point: these supposed well-paid green jobs don’t actually exist.
Sure, there are jobs that can be labelled as green if you don’t mind twisting the definitions a little. The Office for National Statistics had a stab at calculating how many last year, and came up with what it admitted was an “experimental” figure of 639,000 across the whole of the British economy, a surprisingly small number given there are 34m jobs in total.
There are extra jobs being created putting up the wind turbines off the Yorkshire coast – at least when they are not cancelled, as the huge Hornsea 4 wind farm was earlier this month – plus installing solar panels in supermarket car parks and putting up all the extra pylons that will be needed to secure the grid against blackouts.
But any reasonable calculation of the total has to factor in the job losses in the North Sea, as all the people who used to supply the country with conventional fuels. Even more importantly, it has to factor in all the job losses in manufacturing as whole industries get wiped out by sky-high energy prices.
Even the climate change groups protesting this week agree that 227,000 jobs have been lost in the last decade in fossil fuels. Likewise, it is estimated that 600,000 jobs have been lost in manufacturing in the UK over the last decade, and if we attribute at least half of that total to energy costs (which, if we are being honest is probably an underestimate), that means another 300,000 have been sacrificed to net zero.
Add the two figures together and more than 500,000 jobs have been lost, meaning that only a little over 100,000 net green jobs have been created.
Even worse, many of those are simply installation work for technologies such as heat pumps. All they do is simply replace existing work in traditional engineering. If a plumber switches from installing gas boilers to heat pumps he might be classified as moving into a “green job”. But that doesn’t mean any extra employment has been created.
The blunt reality is this. Ed Miliband, along with the climate commissars around him, have been peddling a lie. If there were genuinely lots of well-paid green jobs, we would have seen evidence of them by now.
Instead, we are now in the absurd position where climate groups such as Greenpeace clamour for one round of subsidies for green energy and then another round to help all the people who lose their jobs as a result. It is a never-ending cycle of more and more government spending.
We are lectured endlessly about how transitioning to net zero will create lots of employment. But there is no sign of it actually happening.
Sure, we can all argue about whether climate change is an emergency, or whether it is a problem that can be solved fairly easily with better technology. We can also debate whether the UK really needs to be a world leader in reducing carbon emissions, given that we account for less than 1pc of the global total.
But there is no point in kidding ourselves that the transition is going to make us richer. Right now it is becoming painfully clear that it is throwing lots of people out of work – and there are very few genuinely new jobs being created to compensate for that.

image.caption: Greenpeace and trade unions are demanding the Government finds new jobs for oil workers
